newsitem.title: USA: Senate funds probe focuses on ties to China.
newsitem.headline: Senate funds probe focuses on ties to China.

text.p: A Senate probe into political fund-raising scandals opened on Tuesday with a allegation by its Republican chairman that China planned to buy its way into American politics.

The Senate Governmental Affairs Committee also received a surprise offer of testimony by a key player in the tangled web of donations, John Huang. His lawyer said Huang agreed to speak "truthfully to the best of his knowledge and honest recollection" if given limited immunity from prosecution.

Committee Chairman Fred Thompson of Tennessee, who sharpened his prosecutorial skills as Republican counsel during the Senate Watergate hearings two decades ago, said the first witness on Wednesday would be Richard Sullivan, former finance director for the Democratic National Commitee.

President Bill Clinton, whose popularity has remained high despite a seemingly endless stream of revelations about fund raising, declined to comment. In Madrid, Spain, for a meeting on NATO expansion, he said only: "I can't comment on it. I've been working here."

White House special counsel Lanny Davis issued a neutral, one-sentence statement after the first day of hearings: "We support all efforts of the committee to bring out all the facts concerning campaign finance problems in both parties."
Thompson began the long-awaited, televised hearings with a statement that Beijing's communist leaders had a plan to build political influence in the United States, a charge China has denied.
"The committee believes that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to increase China's influence over the U.S. political process," he said.
At a later news conference, Thompson said he had seen evidence gathered by the FBI of China's continuing efforts to influence U.S. officials but would not make details public.

Apart from foreign influence, the panel over the next four weeks will examine reports of sleepovers in the White House Lincoln Bedroom for campaign high rollers, alleged calls to solicit funds made from the White House by Clinton and Vice President Al Gore, and Gore's attendance at a fund-raiser in a Buddhist temple with monks who had taken a vow of poverty.

Senators of both parties decried the bending of campaign finance laws in the last elections. The more than $600 million spent in the 1996 congressional and presidential campaigns -- nearly 50 percent more than the 1991-92 cycle -- broke all records.

Of China's actions in the 1996 campaign, Thompson said the plan to gain political influence in the United States was drawn up to respond to advances by Taiwan in building influence in Washington and included "typical appropriate" measures like hiring lobbyists and making diplomatic visits.
But he said Beijing had shown an interest in "developing long-term relationships with persons it has identified as up-and-coming officials at state and local levels."
"The intent is to establish relations that can be cultivated as the officials rise through the ranks to higher office," he said.
"The government of China is believed to have allocated substantial sums of money to achieve its objectives," Thompson said.

Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the panel's senior Democrat, warned against a "jump to conclusions," asking, "Is there any real evidence that the Chinese government, or any other foreign government, actually infiltrated the American government via campaign contributions?"

Huang is a central figure in the investigation of domestic and foreign contributions, and his offer to testify will be considered, Thompson said, if he wants to give "full, complete and truthful" testimony.
"If he has hatched a plan to absolve himself while at the same time covering for his friends, we are not interested in that," he added.
Former senior White House and Democratic Party aides are among the potential first witnesses to be called on Wednesday, but two other key figures have fled the country.

Charles Yah Lin Trie, a former Arkansas restaurateur and Clinton friend who became a major Democratic fund-raiser, was believed to be in Shanghai. He raised or donated $645,000 that the DNC later returned. Pauline Kanchanalak, whose $560,000 donation to the Democrats is being investigated, was thought to be in Thailand.
A White House official who asked to remain unidentified pointedly criticized the committee's investigation into Republican fund raising through a separate policy group.

"It is shocking to have heard that the president of the Republican National Policy Forum was allowed to refuse to answer more than 100 questions," the official said. The forum provided funds to the party by way of a loan from a Hong Kong firm.
